title: The Earrings of Aditi
story:
Garuda, the great eagle who carried Krishna, flew up toward heaven bearing a strange cargo: the umbrella of Varuna, lord of the waters, and the jewel mountain — both recovered from a demon's hoard — and on his back Krishna himself, who had come to give back what had been stolen. The great bird went lightly, as if in sport — as though carrying a god to his own house required no effort at all.

At the gates of heaven Krishna blew his conch, and the gods came out to meet him, bearing respectful offerings for the one who had won back their treasures. He passed through their courts, past palaces whose towers rose like white clouds, to the dwelling of the mother of the gods. There sat Aditi — mother of Indra, mother of the gods themselves, the eldest of all the divine mothers — and in her keeping, once, had been the earrings that the demon Narakasura had torn away in his raids on heaven. Krishna bowed before her, with Indra beside him, placed the earrings back in her hands, and told her that the demon who had robbed her was dead.

The mother of the gods was well pleased. She fixed her whole mind on Krishna, and her words came out as praise — long and wondering. He was the one who removes fear from all who worship him, she said; the soul of every living thing, and its beginning. He was evening, night, and day; earth, sky, air, water, and fire; mind, thought, and the sense of self. He was Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, the three great gods; gods and demons and serpents, men and beasts and trees; the vast and the minute — all things that exist, down to the smallest part. And beyond all of this, she said, lay a form no eye could rest on: the deathless one behind every shape the world shows us, whom she could only glimpse and name. Yet the world itself was his play. The feeling that 'I am, this is mine' was a dream he had woven, and only those who worshipped him could pass through that dream into freedom. It was a fault, she added gently, to ask small things of one who could give everything — like asking a wish-fulfilling tree for a rag when it could grant any treasure at all.

So Aditi hymned him, and Krishna smiled. 'Mother,' he said, 'show me favour. Grant me your blessing.' And Aditi answered, 'So be it. While you dwell among mortals, you shall be invincible to gods and demons alike.'

Then Satyabhama, Krishna's wife, came forward, with Indra's queen beside her, and asked the mother of the gods for her blessing as well. Aditi looked at her and smiled. 'Fair-browed one,' she said, 'you shall never suffer decay, nor loss of beauty. You shall be the refuge of all loveliness.'

So the earrings were restored, and blessings passed between them in both directions — the mother of the gods hymning Krishna as the source of all things, and Krishna asking her blessing like a son. When it was done, Indra led his guests through Nandana and the pleasant groves of heaven, where the trees bloomed in gold and copper and the air hung heavy with fragrance. There the Parijata stood among the rest — the golden tree that had risen from the ocean when the gods churned it. Behind them, the mother of the gods held her earrings once more; ahead of them, the gardens of heaven opened, bright and endless.
reflection: The scene turns on exchanged reverence: the mother of the gods hymns Krishna as the origin of all things, and he in turn asks her blessing, and she grants him invincibility. Aditi's praise carries the story's theology in miniature — the creator is also the play of his own illusion — but it is her small, human-sized blessing to Satyabhama, a promise of beauty that will never fade, that lingers longest.
tradition_note: This account follows the Vishnu Purana's telling, in which the earrings are restored after Narakasura's fall. The Bhagavata Purana places the restoration at the end of the same war, with the visit to heaven leading directly into the uprooting of the Parijata tree.
next_story_tease: The earrings had been only one of the stolen treasures, and the city that hoarded the rest still stood unbroken.
hero_scene: Krishna kneeling before Aditi, the mother of the gods, and placing her recovered earrings into her hands while Indra stands beside him and the palace turrets rise like white clouds behind them.
